themes.name: The Physics Rabbit Hole
themes.tagline: From the minus sign in spacetime to why the whole field might need a rethink — physics that actually messes with your head.

items.title: Faraday's Law Explained Visually #physics #electromagnetism #faradayslaw #maxwellsequations
items.description:
Faraday's Law relates the rate of change of magnetic flux to the induced EMF.  In this short, we build an intuitive, visual understanding of Faraday's Law by looking at several examples. This clip is taken from my latest video on Maxwell's Equations.
Watch the full explanation here:https://youtu.be/wt1KJtD4Qh8?si=LeUgZIbRSL2JmRNB
items.why_watch: A clean, visual walkthrough of Faraday's Law that prioritizes intuition over equations — useful if you've seen the math but never quite felt it click. At under 2.5 minutes, it's a low-cost way to test whether this channel's teaching style works for you before committing to the full Maxwell's Equations video.

items.why_watch: This video tackles a question most physics explainers sidestep entirely: why does the spacetime interval have a minus sign, and what does that actually tell us about the nature of time? FloatHead builds the argument carefully from first principles, making it accessible without stripping out the substance.

items.title: Can Physics be Fixed? The 2025 Conference for Physical & Mathematical Ontology
items.description: The 2025 Conference for Physical and Mathematical Ontology took place at the end of June 2025, and saw a number of talented and independent thinkers from all across the globe converge in the city of Munich, Germany. Recognizing the need to restore the lost connection between physics and philosophy, and eschewing the overly-abstract interpretations of modern theories in favor of physically grounded, cause-and-effect models, these individuals set out to explore some of the deepest mysteries of our
items.why_watch: A ground-level look at a conference deliberately pushing back against the philosophy-free, shut-up-and-calculate culture that has dominated theoretical physics — featuring independent researchers, not just institutional voices. If you've wondered whether the foundational questions in physics are being seriously revisited anywhere, this gives you a concrete answer.

themes.name: Trust, But Verify
themes.tagline: What happens when the systems we rely on — courtrooms, consensus, institutions — were built on shakier ground than anyone admitted.

items.title: We've Been Using The Wrong Science In Court For 50 years
items.description:

Last year, we launched the Elements of Truth game on Kickstarter and were thrilled by the response. We’re now in the final stages of production, with Kickstarter rewards shipping soon. If you missed the campaign, you can now pre-order the retail edition through our new website here - https://ve42.c
items.why_watch: Veritasium examines how forensic techniques like bite-mark analysis and hair matching — long treated as courtroom gold standards — were adopted without rigorous scientific validation, and how that failure has contributed to wrongful convictions. It's a sobering look at what happens when the legal system mistakes expert confidence for empirical proof.

themes.name: Under The Hood
themes.tagline: For the tinkerers and the curious — what's really happening inside the machine, one instruction at a time.

items.title: ALU instruction SIMULATION - Control Unit - Scott's CPU - How computers work
items.description:
In this video we start to see the instruction code of the Scott’s CPU. In particular the ALU instruction. We see the control logic to drive the ALU instruction. This video is the simulation part of the theoretical video «Instruction code - ALU instruction» of the «How computers work – building Scott’s CPU» youtube playlist. The link to the playlist and the circuitVerse link are in description.

How Computers work playlist : https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLnAxReCloSeTJc8ZGogzjtCtXl_eE6yzA&si=
items.why_watch: A niche but genuinely useful video for anyone working through how CPUs execute instructions at the hardware level — specifically how the control unit decodes ALU opcodes in Scott's 8-bit CPU build. The simulation format makes the signal flow far easier to follow than a schematic alone would.

morning_soundtrack.title: Meet the alien math-rock duo selling out shows across the U.S.
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Angine de Poitrine wears giant masks, speaks an alien language and plays wildly complicated math rock. Manager Sebastien Collin talks about the rise of the enigmatic musical group.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like stumbling into a fever dream at 2am where the band is definitely not human but you can't stop nodding your head.

morning_soundtrack.title: Olivia Rodrigo has a lot on her mind. But she's still choosing joy
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Olivia Rodrigo is thinking about joy, falling madly in love and what pop music can do when the world feels overwhelming.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Bubblegum optimism with a bruised heart underneath, like dancing alone in your room after crying.

morning_soundtrack.title: Cell Rot Announce New Album Paradise: Hear “Paradise/Parasite II”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The fast and nasty Oakland hardcore band Cell Rot put out an album called Parasite last year, the first half of a two-part project recorded with the iconic punk and metal producer Jack Shirley. Soon they'll drop the second half, Paradise . On opening track and lead single "Paradise/Parasite II," they hammer home the resemblance between those two words and the relationship between the concepts.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The sound of something rotting beautifully, like a mosh pit in a condemned building.

morning_soundtrack.title: American Motors Announce New Album Functional Music: Hear “No Horses”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Lancaster, PA trio American Motors impressed us with their 2024 debut Content . Now they're back to announce another album of scraping, pounding, ominous underground rock music. For Functional Music , out in November, the band once again recorded with the legendary J Robbins at his Magpie Cage studio in Baltimore, so Alex Steward's drums thwack extra viscerally.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Concrete and rust given a pulse — music that feels like it was recorded inside a collapsing warehouse.

morning_soundtrack.title: Pulp Break Out Deep Cuts They Hadn’t Played In Decades At End Of The Road 2026
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Pulp have been back at it for well over three years now, so it's probably too late to reflexively describe them as "the reunited Pulp" or "the resurgent Pulp." But if it's no longer novel for Jarvis Cocker and friends to be playing shows and releasing new music again, there are still ways for the band to surprise and delight their fans.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The warm shock of hearing a song you forgot you loved being played like it never went away.

morning_soundtrack.title: FOUNDERS KEEPERS: “Do Something…Even If It's Wrong”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Somehow the pacifist child grew up loving pro wrestling, and the 12-inch black and white television didn't even enter the house until the summer of the Watergate hearings, when I had the chainsaw accident. This can now be rationalized as the careful study of how character can
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Sun-worn and strange, like a story told on a porch by someone who's lived too many lives to keep them straight.

morning_soundtrack.title: Radiohead Announce Australia and Japan Shows
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The band will play a total of 21 dates in 2027
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The quiet electricity of circling a date on a calendar and already dreading how much it will mean.

morning_soundtrack.title: Bad Bunny Wins His First Emmy Award
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Puerto Rican star’s Super Bowl LX Halftime Show won all seven categories it was nominated in at the Creative Arts Emmys
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Confetti and a crown — the triumphant, bass-rattling energy of someone who showed up and swept the room.

morning_soundtrack.title: Here’s Everyone Kanye West Brought Out at His Homecoming Chicago Show
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Future, 2 Chainz, Twista, Young Thug, Travis Scott, and more appeared at the embattled rapper’s Windy City stint
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A hometown block party that somehow keeps escalating until half the city is on stage.

morning_soundtrack.title: Upper Wilds :: Mercury
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Dan Friel is having a summer, what with the surprise resurgence of aughts noise mainstays Parts & Labor and now a fourth album from guitar-centric, astronomy-centric Upper Wilds. Yet while the double disc Parts & Labor veered occasionally towards proggy excess Mercury runs a ferociously tight ship. It’s loud as fuck, but nothing’s wasted.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Staring directly into the sun through a guitar amp — blinding, relentless, and somehow clarifying.

morning_soundtrack.title: Macklemore Defends Pro-Palestine Remarks at Ed Sheeran Concert Following Criticism from P!NK, Boy George
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The rapper is standing by his remarks after his MetLife Stadium speech drew criticism and calls for his removal from Sheeran's tour. Macklemore Defends Pro-Palestine Remarks at Ed Sheeran Concert Following Criticism from P!NK, Boy George Alex Young
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The charged, uncomfortable silence after someone grabs the mic and says what nobody at the party wanted to hear.

morning_soundtrack.title: Jeff Arcuri on Netflix Stand-Up Special Nice to Meet You and Escaping the Crowd Work Box: Podcast
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The comedian reveals why he couldn’t watch the finished set for a month, how therapy helped him return to it, and what he’s writing next. Jeff Arcuri on Netflix Stand-Up Special Nice to Meet You and Escaping the Crowd Work Box: Podcast Kyle Meredith
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The nervous laugh of finally watching back footage of yourself being completely vulnerable and realizing it was worth it.

global_silver_linings.title: Good News in History, September 8
global_silver_linings.snippet: 60 years ago, the first episode of Star Trek, featuring “Space: the final frontier” and the USS Enterprise, began its three-year mission of exploration on TV screens across America. The science-fiction television show created by Gene Roddenberry was set in the 23rd century and starred William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy. The NBC show has since […]
global_silver_linings.reason: History is full of quiet victories worth remembering — pausing to mark the good that has happened on this day reminds us that progress is real and has always been possible. These moments of reflection root us in a longer story of human resilience.

global_silver_linings.title: Forget how your mom did it. There’s actually a right way to remove a tick.
global_silver_linings.snippet: No matches, alcohol, or Vaseline—and for good reason.
global_silver_linings.reason: Updated, evidence-based guidance on tick removal means fewer people are accidentally making a bad situation worse outdoors — a small but genuinely useful piece of knowledge that keeps families safer in the garden and on the trail.

global_silver_linings.title: The neuroscience of motivation: what orexin neurons reveal about staying the course
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Nagoya University identified orexin-producing neurons as the brain’s apparent mechanism for deciding whether a reward is worth pursuing. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study suggests these cells are doing something more specific than previously understood: not just regulating wakefulness and energy, but […] The post The neuroscience of motivation: what orexin neurons reveal about staying the course first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Scientists are uncovering the specific brain circuits that help us push through difficulty, offering real insight into why motivation falters and how we might support it more effectively. Understanding the biology of perseverance is a meaningful step toward helping people live with more purpose and less unnecessary struggle.

featured_read.title: Why We Like Things
featured_read.snippet: What Silicon Valley gets wrong about taste.
featured_read.blurb: This essay picks a fight with the recommendation algorithm, arguing that Silicon Valley has confused preference data with taste—and that the difference matters more than we've admitted. A sharp, clarifying read for anyone who has felt vaguely betrayed by their own Spotify Wrapped.

reading_room.title: Much Ado About Adenoids
reading_room.snippet: Much Ado About Adenoids : Edmund Lawall must have felt cursed. He’d brought his family to New York in the late 1800s to carry on his father’s business as a pharmacist, but fate—or perhaps the city itself—seemed determined to drive him back out again. Lawall’s health had been in decline since their arrival, and his wife’s kidney disease had worsened, […]
reading_room.blurb: One pharmacist's relentless health troubles in late-1800s New York become the unlikely entry point into a strange and forgotten chapter of medical history, where a single small piece of throat tissue was blamed for nearly everything wrong with the modern body. Curl up with this one if you enjoy the kind of story where medicine looks, in hindsight, like inspired guesswork.

reading_room.title: Continental divide
reading_room.snippet: A century ago, the Pan-American road promised a new era of fraternity between the two continents. Did it succeed? - by Shawn Miller Read on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: The Pan-American Highway was sold as a ribbon of continental brotherhood stretching from Alaska to Patagonia—this essay asks what happened to that dream when rubber met the road, and why the gap in the Darién jungle tells a truer story than any ribbon-cutting ever did.

reading_room.title: What Archaeology Reveals About the Rise of All-Powerful Rulers
reading_room.snippet: Autocracy wasn’t inevitable in early civilizations—many were more egalitarian. But when riches were there to monopolize, strongmen and inequalities emerged
reading_room.blurb: Autocracy, it turns out, needed the right conditions to take root—and archaeologists are now reading its origin story in the soil. This is an unsettling and clarifying look at the precise moment, repeated across early civilizations, when surplus became leverage and one person figured out how to own both.

reading_room.title: Is it morally wrong to not take care of yourself?
reading_room.snippet: The philosophical debate goes on. But our research on self-obligations suggests there’s a common, consequential view - by Laura K Soter & Fan Yang Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Most ethical philosophy worries about what we owe each other, but this essay quietly presses on the neglected question of what we owe ourselves—and whether neglecting your own wellbeing is not just unwise but actually wrong. It's the kind of piece that stays with you the next time you skip the thing you know would do you good.

reading_room.title: On Tour with the Eclipse Chasers
reading_room.snippet: "They spend their lives seeking seconds of darkness."
reading_room.blurb: Eclipse chasers rearrange their entire lives around two minutes of totality—this piece gets close enough to understand why that trade feels not just reasonable, but necessary. A rare portrait of obsession that makes you want to book a flight instead of an appointment.

garden_note.note: There's a particular quality to early September mornings in Zürich — the air has that first cool edge, almost mineral, as the light arrives a little later each day and the lindens begin their quiet surrender. Step out around first light and you'll catch the garden at its most honest: dew on the late-summer chard, spiders at work on their dewy threads, and the first few leaves on the ornamental vines already blushing amber.

Swiss chard and kale ready for harvest; cut outer leaves to keep plants productive
Apple and early pear trees dropping their first windfalls — check daily and press or store promptly

news.blurb: A spice rack that earns its keep after years of daily use is the kind of quiet kitchen wisdom worth a peek.

news.title: ‘Still or Sparkling’ Must Be Stopped
news.snippet: All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to release the pressure valve of crankiness that comes with sweating your way through the end of summer. This story was previously published as part of that series. Subscribe to Eater Today to see more of our editors’ boldest opinions […]
news.blurb: Someone finally said it out loud, and honestly, the water ritual at restaurants deserves every word of this spirited takedown.

news.title: José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
news.snippet: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing One of my favourite summer memories is making collares de moras as a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces. We’d always eat some too, of course, as well as wearing them, and we’d always come home with stained hands and big smiles. At the time, I never imagined that one day I’d be cooking sardines and pairing them with those same wild berries, but that’s the magic of food.
news.blurb: Grilled sardines meet a blackberry escabeche in what sounds like the most poetic argument for eating seasonally at the tail end of summer.

recipe.title: Fennel Mushrooms
recipe.snippet: A fennel mushroom recipe inspired by one of my vintage cookbooks, The Seasonal Kitchen by Perla Meyers. It's a simple, brilliant twist on everyday sauteed mushrooms with dill, chives, fresh fennel, and a kiss of creme fraiche.
recipe.blurb: These fennel mushrooms — fragrant with fresh fennel, dill, and chives — are the kind of effortlessly elegant weeknight side that makes an ordinary Tuesday feel quietly special.

larder.seasonal_note: Zürich's Tuesday and Saturday markets at Bürkliplatz are piled with Berner Rosen and Gravenstein apples right now — slice one thin over a warm Birchermüesli this morning, and the whole kitchen smells like the season turning.

fern_data.greeting: If the wrong forensic science has been steering courtrooms for fifty years, what else are we certain of that we shouldn't be? Today also has the neuroscience of why you want anything at all — which feels like a useful companion question.
